newsitem.title: USA: Feb. U.S. auto sales seen off slightly, still firm.
newsitem.headline: Feb. U.S. auto sales seen off slightly, still firm.

text.p: Automakers are expected to report Monday that U.S. light vehicle sales in February declined slightly from unusually strong results last year, and Japanese brands continued to gain market share.
Severe winter storms in January 1996 delayed a considerable number of vehicle purchases until February, making comparisons with February 1997 more difficult.
Despite the declines, however, Wall Street analysts said the industry's seasonally adjusted annual sales rate for February will remain strong, at about 15.5 million to 15.7 million light vehicles.
Americans bought light vehicles at a 15.8 million-unit rate in February 1996 and at a 15.5 million unit rate in January 1997.

Sales for General Motors Corp. are forecast to be down six to seven percent, mainly due to shortages of key light truck models, coupled with continuing launches of new car models that are not yet widely available at dealerships.
Ford Motor Co sales are expected to be flat to down 1 percent, with light truck sales up five percent and passenger car sales down seven percent.
Dean Witter Reynolds Inc analyst Ronald Glantz said Ford car sales were off because the company has opted not to offer generous incentives on its Escort and Tracer small cars.
Chrysler Corp sales are expected to be flat to up two percent compared with last year, also with an increase in truck sales offset by a decline in car sales.
"Chrysler's car sales are down because its Neon, Stratus, Breeze and Cirrus are being eaten alive by the Japanese," Glantz said.
Japanese automakers, especially Toyota Motor Corp. and Honda Motor Co. Ltd, are expected to gain market share again in February, but at a slower pace than they did in January.

Burnham Securities analyst David Healy said in a research report that foreign brands captured 27.2 percent of the total U.S. vehicle market in February, up sharply from 23.8 percent a year earlier, but down slightly from 28.5 percent in January.

"Anecdotes from the real world suggest that the Japnese producers are taking advantage of the weak yen and strong dollar and gaining market share at the expense of GM, Ford and Chrysler via aggressive price competition, especially in intermediate and compact-sized cars," Healy said in the report.
He estimates that sales of U.S.-made Japanese cars in February will be up about 9 percent over year-ago levels.
GM and Chrysler are expected to report their February U.S. sales data on Monday, March 3, while Ford plans to report its sales on Tuesday.
